# Icechunk: a versioned store {#sec-icechunk}

```{r}
#| include: false
source("R/book.R")
```

[Icechunk](https://icechunk.io) puts a transaction log in front of Zarr:
snapshots, branches and tags, so a reader can pin a version and keep
reading it while writers move on. Chunks are found through the snapshot's
manifest, not by key, and a chunk can be native (stored in the
repository), inline, or virtual (a byte range of a file somewhere else).

In R, [tabularberg](https://github.com/hypertidy/tabularberg) wraps the
Icechunk Rust library, and zaro opens a repository as a store.

## A seal, and the ocean model under it

Two virtual stores on
[Source Cooperative](https://source.coop/ausantarctic/ausantarctic-scratch),
both built with
[raad.virtualize](https://github.com/mdsumner/raad.virtualize) and
published as Icechunk repositories among other forms. Neither holds a
copy of the data.

- **IMOS seal CTD profiles**
  ([`imos-tracking/meop-ctd-2024`](https://source.coop/ausantarctic/ausantarctic-scratch/imos-tracking)).
  Elephant seals, Weddell seals and fur seals carry satellite-relay CTD
  tags, and each dive is a temperature and salinity profile at one place
  and time. The 2024 release is 126,518 profiles of 1000 levels, in 265
  classic netCDF files in the IMOS public bucket. The repository presents
  them as one cube, each profile a chunk: 4000 bytes of one of those
  files.
- **Bluelink (BRAN) temperature**
  ([`bluelink/bluelink-daily-temp`](https://source.coop/ausantarctic/ausantarctic-scratch/bluelink)).
  The reanalysis of @sec-virtual, daily from 1993, every chunk a byte
  range of a netCDF file on NCI's THREDDS server.

```r
coop <- "https://data.source.coop/ausantarctic/ausantarctic-scratch/"
meop <- zaro_icechunk(paste0(coop, "imos-tracking/meop-ctd-2024/icechunk"),
                      authorize = "https://", direct = TRUE)
meop@snapshot                  # the version this store is pinned to
obs  <- zaro_array(meop, "TEMP_ADJUSTED", cf = TRUE)   # level, profile
bran <- zaro(paste0("flatrefs://", coop, "bluelink/bluelink-daily-temp/flat"))
temp <- zaro_array(bran, "temp", cf = TRUE)            # x, y, depth, day
```

::: {.callout-important}
The model is not read through Icechunk here yet. zaro's Icechunk store
loads the whole reference table of an array before it looks up a chunk.
For the seal cube that is 126,518 rows. For Bluelink temperature it is
37.5 million, and the first render of this chapter ran out of memory
there, in both builds. Each Bluelink dataset is published in several
forms from the same references, so this chapter reads the flat Parquet
form, which zaro reads one row group at a time. The Icechunk read needs
zaro to ask for only the manifest rows a request covers.
:::

The job: take five dives of one seal on the Kerguelen plateau in 2019,
and for each get what the seal measured and what the model has at that
cell on that day. In R that is two lines. What the seal measured is a
block of a matrix, `obs[, dives]`. What the model has is a profile,
`temp[i, j, , t]`, for each dive: 51 chunks, one per depth level.

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| eval: false
#| file: scripts/06-icechunk.R
```

```{r}
res <- book_run("06-icechunk.R", live = TRUE)
book_table(res)
```

Three hosts are involved in these reads: Source Cooperative for the
references, the IMOS bucket in Sydney for the seal profiles, NCI in
Canberra for the model. On stock R every chunk from either archive is its
own round trip, in series. With the method, each `[` is one batch.

The third row is the workaround a careful user can write today: build
the index matrix for every level of every dive by hand, and R passes it
through whole in both builds. It is the fastest of the three, and it is
the code nobody writes first.

```{r}
book_elt(res)
```

```{r}
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 3.6
#| fig-cap: "Temperature profiles from five dives of one seal (line), and the BRAN temperature at the same cell and day (points)."
f <- "results/06-dives.csv"
if (file.exists(f)) {
  d <- utils::read.csv(f, stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
  n <- max(d$dive)
  op <- par(mfrow = c(1, n), mar = c(4, 3, 2.5, 0.5), mgp = c(1.8, 0.6, 0))
  for (v in seq_len(n)) {
    s <- d[d$dive == v & d$source == "seal", ]
    m <- d[d$dive == v & d$source == "model", ]
    zmax <- max(s$depth, 100)
    m <- m[m$depth <= zmax * 1.1, ]
    plot(s$temp, s$depth, type = "l", col = "steelblue", lwd = 2,
         ylim = c(zmax, 0), xlim = range(c(s$temp, m$temp)),
         xlab = "deg C", ylab = if (v == 1) "depth (m, dbar)" else "",
         main = d$label[d$dive == v][1], cex.main = 0.85)
    points(m$temp, m$depth, pch = 19, cex = 0.7, col = "firebrick")
  }
  par(op)
}
```

::: {.callout-note}
tabularberg needs a Rust toolchain to build; the book image includes it
unless built with `WITH_ICECHUNK=false` (@sec-rebuild), and without it
this chapter has no table. Requests to THREDDS are capped at 4 at a time.
The Source Cooperative location is a scratch area: datasets are added
there over time.
:::

## Why the batch matters more here

With a plain Zarr store a chunk's address is its key. With Icechunk each
chunk is looked up in a manifest, and a virtual chunk then points at
another host. A reader given the whole request resolves all the
references in one pass over the manifest and can group the fetches by
host. A reader given one element at a time does that lookup once per
chunk. The deeper the indirection, the more a store gains from being
asked once.
